title: Meditations on First Philosophy
author: René Descartes
openingChapterLabel: Meditation I — Of the Things of Which We May Doubt
openingText: Several years have now elapsed since I first became aware that I had accepted, even from my youth, many false opinions for true, and that consequently what I afterward based on such principles was highly doubtful; and from that time I was convinced of the necessity of undertaking once in my life to rid myself of all the opinions I had adopted, and of commencing anew the work of building from the foundation, if I desired to establish a firm and abiding superstructure in the sciences. But as this enterprise appeared to me to be one of great magnitude, I waited until I had attained an age so mature as to leave me no hope that at any stage of life more advanced I should be better able to execute my design. To-day, then, since I have opportunely freed my mind from all cares and am happily disturbed by no passions, and since I am in the secure possession of leisure in a peaceable retirement, I will at length apply myself earnestly and freely to the general overthrow of all my former opinions.
about:
The Meditations on First Philosophy is Descartes's six-day attempt to rebuild knowledge from scratch. Doubting everything that can be doubted, he arrives at one certainty — "I think, therefore I am" — and from there tries to prove the existence of God, the reliability of the senses, and the distinction between mind and body. The book is short, structured as six daily meditations, and meant to be read slowly.

Descartes published it in 1641. It is the founding text of modern philosophy. Every subsequent debate about the relationship between mind and body, between knowledge and doubt, between self and world is shaped by what Descartes attempted in these six days.

angleCards.title: Methodical doubt as a tool.
angleCards.text: Descartes does not doubt out of pessimism — he doubts as a surgical method. Whatever survives total demolition must be solid enough to build on. Follow what he actually doubts and why, and notice what survives each round of destruction.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what methodical doubt actually achieves — how deliberate, extreme scepticism can become the foundation for knowledge rather than its enemy.

angleCards.title: The Cogito and the foundation move.
angleCards.text: "I think, therefore I am" is not an argument — it is a performance. You cannot doubt that doubting is happening. From this single indubitable point Descartes tries to rebuild the entire edifice of knowledge. Watch whether the reconstruction holds.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the Cogito as a philosophical move — how one certain point is used to anchor a whole worldview, and whether the reconstruction from that anchor actually works.

angleCards.title: The mind-body problem.
angleCards.text: Descartes concludes that mind and body are entirely different substances — one thinking and unextended, the other extended and unthinking. This is the dualism that philosophy has been arguing about ever since. He invents the problem as clearly as anyone ever has.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read for the moment Descartes separates mind from body — and understand why that distinction seemed forced and what problems it immediately creates.

angleCards.title: God as the guarantor of knowledge.
angleCards.text: Before Descartes can trust his own clear and distinct ideas — even his mathematics — he needs to prove that a good God exists who is not deceiving him. Notice the order: the Cogito comes first, then God, then the world. The sequence matters enormously.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand why Descartes needs to prove God's existence before he can trust his own reasoning — and whether the famous circularity in that argument is fatal or survivable.

cast.name: Methodical Doubt
cast.description: Not scepticism as a conclusion but as a technique. Descartes resolves to reject anything he can find even a slight reason to doubt, until he locates something that survives every challenge. The method drives the entire inquiry.

cast.name: Cogito Ergo Sum
cast.description: "I think, therefore I am." The one point the doubting method cannot dissolve — because the act of doubting is itself a form of thinking, and thinking requires a thinker. The fulcrum on which all of modern philosophy rests.

cast.name: Clear and Distinct Ideas
cast.description: Descartes' criterion for what we can know with certainty: whatever we perceive clearly and distinctly must be true. God's existence is required to guarantee this rule holds — otherwise an evil demon could be making false things seem obvious.

cast.name: The Evil Demon
cast.description: What if an all-powerful deceiver were feeding us every experience, every mathematical intuition, every apparent certainty — all false? The demon is not a real belief but a tool: if something survives even this hypothesis, it is truly indubitable.

cast.name: Mind and Body
cast.description: Descartes concludes that the mind — a thinking, unextended thing — is entirely distinct from the body — an extended, unthinking thing. The problem of how these two radically different substances interact is the wound modern philosophy has been trying to close ever since.

cast.name: The Cartesian Circle
cast.description: Descartes uses clear and distinct ideas to prove God, then uses God to guarantee that clear and distinct ideas are reliable. Critics immediately spotted the circularity. Whether it is vicious or survivable is one of the oldest debates in the history of philosophy.

whyItMatters.title: The First Modern Philosophy
whyItMatters.body: Descartes broke with the medieval tradition of starting from authority — Aristotle, the Church Fathers — and started from himself. The first-person philosophical method, beginning from one's own consciousness and trying to build outward, starts here.

whyItMatters.title: "I Think, Therefore I Am"
whyItMatters.body: The phrase has become famous to the point of cliché. Reading the Meditations restores it. Descartes arrives at the cogito after pages of methodical doubt; the line is the bottom of a deep dive, not a slogan.

whyItMatters.title: The Mind-Body Problem
whyItMatters.body: The book's claim that mind and body are different substances — and the question of how they could possibly interact — is the founding problem of modern philosophy of mind. Three and a half centuries of work on consciousness, neuroscience, and AI are still working in its shadow.
